Frank Sinatra: Frank Sinatra brought effortless swing and unmistakable style to classics including “My Way” and “Fly Me to the Moon”. His Christmas recordings bring that same warmth to the festive season, with “White Christmas” providing a wonderfully nostalgic moment. Smooth vocals, a little old-school glamour and absolutely no novelty jumper required.
Taylor Swift: Taylor Swift grew from country storyteller into a global pop star, with songs including “Love Story” and “Shake It Off” inspiring enormous singalongs. Her festive repertoire includes “Santa Baby”, recorded for The Taylor Swift Holiday Collection. It’s a playful seasonal detour — even a pop superstar has a Christmas wish list.
Chris De Burgh: Chris de Burgh has a gift for turning songs into stories, from the mysterious “Don’t Pay the Ferryman” to his romantic ballads. “A Spaceman Came Travelling” takes that storytelling somewhere rather unexpected, imagining a visitor from beyond the stars. A thoughtful Christmas tale, with a different sort of flying visitor to the usual sleigh.
Pet Shop Boys: Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe brought thoughtful lyrics and electronic pop together in Pet Shop Boys, breaking through with “West End Girls”. Their seasonal contribution, “It Doesn’t Often Snow at Christmas”, keeps that dry wit intact. It’s a Christmas song with dancing shoes on and a refreshingly realistic view of the British weather.
Gwen Stefani: Gwen Stefani first made her mark fronting No Doubt, whose “Don’t Speak” became a huge hit, before building a solo pop career. Her album You Make It Feel Like Christmas brings that distinctive voice to seasonal songs, including a title-track duet with Blake Shelton. Expect a cheerful meeting of pop energy and traditional Christmas sounds.
The Jackson 5: The Jackson 5 brought youthful energy and tightly woven harmonies to Motown, with “I Want You Back” and “ABC” introducing their sound to a huge audience. Their Christmas Album gives familiar songs the same lively treatment. On “Santa Claus Is Coming to Town”, the excitement sounds less like waiting patiently and more like counting every last minute.
John Lennon: John Lennon helped shape pop music with the Beatles before pursuing a solo career that included “Imagine”. Written with Yoko Ono, “Happy Xmas (War Is Over)” brings together their voices, the Plastic Ono Band and the Harlem Community Choir. Its seasonal greeting carries a serious wish for peace, making room for reflection among the celebrations.
Johnny Mathis: Johnny Mathis built his career on romantic ballads and a voice that makes even a familiar melody feel intimate. Christmas became an important part of his repertoire, with “When a Child Is Born” reaching the UK Christmas number one spot in 1976. It’s a gentle, hopeful performance for a quieter moment in a busy season.
Queen: Queen made rock music theatrical, adventurous and wonderfully singable, with Freddie Mercury’s voice at the centre of songs such as “Bohemian Rhapsody”. Their 1984 single “Thank God It’s Christmas” offers a more reflective celebration. There’s still plenty of feeling in the performance, but this time the invitation is to pause rather than stomp along.
Sam Ryder: Sam Ryder’s soaring voice carried “Space Man” to the Eurovision stage and helped introduce his debut album, There’s Nothing But Space, Man! His festive single “You’re Christmas to Me” swaps the cosmic setting for something closer to home. It’s an exuberant celebration of togetherness, delivered with enough enthusiasm to brighten a rather grey December afternoon.
Blossoms: Blossoms are the Stockport band whose self-titled debut album reached number one in 2016. Their melodic indie-pop also has a winter wardrobe: “It’s Going to Be a Cold Winter” arrived alongside “Christmas Eve (Soul Purpose)”. It’s a seasonal change of scenery for the band, with their knack for a memorable tune still firmly in place.
Aled Jones: Aled Jones became a familiar voice at Christmas with his 1985 recording of “Walking in the Air”, later building a career in singing and broadcasting. His hit version is separate from Peter Auty’s original performance in The Snowman. That clear, floating melody still offers a little escape from the bustle below, without anyone needing to leave the sofa.
Bon Jovi: Bon Jovi built their reputation on big rock choruses, with Jon Bon Jovi leading the band through hits including “Livin’ on a Prayer”. “Christmas Isn’t Christmas” takes a gentler approach, reflecting on how much the people around us matter at this time of year. It’s a heartfelt change of pace from the stadium singalongs.
The Darkness: The Darkness brought extravagant guitar rock back into the spotlight with Permission to Land and “I Believe in a Thing Called Love”. Their festive single “Christmas Time (Don’t Let the Bells End)” applies the same larger-than-life approach to December. Subtle it isn’t, but sometimes the Christmas playlist has room for a guitar solo as well as a carol.
Wham!: George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley made Wham! a defining pop duo of the 1980s, with hits including “Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go”. George wrote “Last Christmas”, pairing a bright melody with a bruised-hearted story. Released in 1984, it became a seasonal favourite long before finally claiming the UK Christmas number one spot in 2023.
Greg Lake: Greg Lake’s voice and musicianship were central to King Crimson and Emerson, Lake & Palmer. His solo single “I Believe in Father Christmas” brings that progressive-rock background to a thoughtful look at childhood wonder and adult expectations. Behind the grand arrangement is something more searching than a simple festive greeting, and all the more memorable for it.
Spice Girls: The Spice Girls made “Wannabe” a calling card for their exuberant brand of pop, then became regular visitors to the Christmas charts. Their version of the Waitresses’ “Christmas Wrapping” appeared on the “Goodbye” single. It’s a lively seasonal side trip from a group whose songs rarely require much encouragement to get a singalong started.
Kelly Clarkson & Ariana Grande: Kelly Clarkson and Ariana Grande each have a substantial pop career and a distinctive Christmas repertoire. They join forces on “Santa, Can’t You Hear Me”, recorded for Clarkson’s When Christmas Comes Around… album. This is a collaboration, not a new group: two expressive voices trading lines and meeting in harmonies that give the seasonal wish list extra lift.
The Ronettes: The Ronettes helped define 1960s girl-group pop, with Ronnie Spector’s distinctive lead voice making “Be My Baby” instantly recognisable. Their recording of “Sleigh Ride” brings that same spirited character to Christmas. Bright harmonies and a bustling arrangement make this a lively trip through the snow, with no need to check the traffic before setting off.
Lindsey Lohan: Lindsay Lohan is known for films including Mean Girls as well as a parallel career in pop music. She returned to “Jingle Bell Rock” for the soundtrack of Falling for Christmas, giving the familiar song a fresh performance. It’s a cheerful connection between her screen work and singing, with a knowing nod to an earlier movie moment.
Mel & Kim: This Mel & Kim pairing is comedian Mel Smith and “Kids in America” singer Kim Wilde, not the Appleby sisters. They teamed up for Comic Relief’s 1987 version of “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree”. The combination of pop vocals and comic mischief gives the old favourite a playful twist: a one-off duet with its tongue firmly in its cheek.
Engelbert Humperdinck: Engelbert Humperdinck made his name with romantic hits such as “Release Me” and “The Last Waltz”. His seasonal repertoire includes “Around the Christmas Tree”, from Warmest Christmas Wishes. The familiar richness of his voice suits a song centred on gathering together, offering a relaxed alternative to the more boisterous corners of the Christmas playlist.
Band Aid: Band Aid brought together a temporary line-up of pop performers for famine relief in Ethiopia. Bob Geldof and Midge Ure wrote “Do They Know It’s Christmas?”, recorded in 1984 with voices including George Michael, Boy George and Bono. This is the original recording, rather than one of the later versions, and a significant moment in music fundraising.
Kelly Clarkson: Kelly Clarkson’s American Idol breakthrough led to a pop career that includes “Since U Been Gone” and “Stronger”. Her Christmas album Wrapped in Red introduced “Underneath the Tree”, co-written with Greg Kurstin. It puts her powerful voice at the centre of a busy, joyful arrangement, making a convincing case for company over anything wrapped in a box.
Chris Rea: Chris Rea combined a distinctive, weathered voice with blues-influenced guitar playing on songs such as “The Road to Hell”. “Driving Home for Christmas” finds him on a rather more welcoming journey. Its unhurried rhythm and everyday observations capture the anticipation of getting back to familiar faces, even when the journey itself takes a little patience.
Ariana Grande: Ariana Grande moved from television into a pop career built on expressive vocals and songs including “Problem” and “Thank U, Next”. Her Christmas Kisses EP includes a fresh take on Wham!’s “Last Christmas”. It brings her own vocal character to a familiar seasonal story, rather than simply following the original recording note for note.
Bastille: Bastille broke through with “Pompeii”, combining Dan Smith’s distinctive voice with a chorus built for communal singing. Their version of Slade’s “Merry Xmas Everybody” brings a familiar Christmas favourite into the band’s repertoire. It’s a chance to hear those well-known words through a different pop voice, while keeping the invitation to join in firmly intact.
Dido: Dido’s quietly distinctive voice helped make No Angel a breakthrough album, with songs including “Thank You” and “Here with Me”. “Christmas Day” offers a story-led seasonal recording rather than a party anthem. Its wintry atmosphere makes a gentle contrast to the bigger choruses around it, inviting you to listen closely for a few minutes.
Carly Rae Jepsen: Carly Rae Jepsen’s “Call Me Maybe” introduced her to a worldwide audience, while albums such as Emotion showed the breadth of her pop songwriting. Her festive song “It’s Not Christmas Till Somebody Cries” takes a wry look at imperfect celebrations. A useful reminder that a family Christmas needn’t resemble a glossy advert to be memorable.
Darlene Love: Darlene Love’s voice is at the heart of “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)”, a recording that balances longing with a rush of energy. Her wider career includes 1960s singles such as “(Today I Met) The Boy I’m Gonna Marry”. At Christmas, that expressive delivery gives even the biggest arrangement a wonderfully human centre.
Coldplay: Coldplay grew from the intimate appeal of “Yellow” into a band associated with expansive songs and communal choruses. Their 2010 single “Christmas Lights” begins in a more troubled mood before opening into hope. It’s a seasonal song that makes room for mixed feelings, with Chris Martin’s voice guiding the move from reflection towards celebration.
Ed Sheeran & Elton John: Ed Sheeran and Elton John bring two generations of British songwriting together on “Merry Christmas”. Released in 2021, their duet reached number one in the UK. Elton’s piano-pop tradition and Ed’s melodic storytelling meet in a song made for sharing, with enough bells and good cheer to make the title feel entirely appropriate.
Kylie Minogue: Kylie Minogue’s pop career stretches from “I Should Be So Lucky” to dance-floor favourites such as “Can’t Get You Out of My Head”. Kylie Christmas brings her playful delivery to seasonal standards and newer songs. “Santa Baby” is a particularly cheeky fit, turning the Christmas wish list into something rather more elaborate than socks.
East 17: East 17 brought a streetwise pop sound to the 1990s, with songs including “House of Love” and “It’s Alright”. Their ballad “Stay Another Day” became the UK Christmas number one in 1994. It wasn’t originally written as a Christmas song, but those bells and the snowy video helped give it a lasting December home.
Shakin Stevens: Shakin’ Stevens brought rock ’n’ roll style to the British pop charts with hits such as “This Ole House” and “Oh Julie”. “Merry Christmas Everyone” became the UK Christmas number one in 1985. Its cheerful bounce makes it a natural party choice, even for anyone whose dancing is usually confined to avoiding the wrapping paper.
Elvis Presley: Elvis Presley brought rock ’n’ roll, country and blues into a distinctive musical mix, alongside a gift for heartfelt ballads. His Christmas recordings show both sides, from lively seasonal songs to the yearning “Blue Christmas”. That familiar voice gives the festive repertoire character without needing every song to turn into a full-scale celebration.
Sia: Sia built a career as both a distinctive singer and a songwriter for other artists, with “Chandelier” becoming one of her signature songs. Everyday Is Christmas brings her melodic instincts to original seasonal material, including “Santa’s Coming for Us”. It’s a colourful alternative to familiar standards, with that unmistakable voice doing much of the decorating.
Jose Feliciano: José Feliciano is a singer and guitarist whose recordings cross pop and Latin music, including his distinctive interpretation of “Light My Fire”. He wrote “Feliz Navidad”, bringing Spanish and English together in a wonderfully direct Christmas greeting. Its appeal is easy to understand: a warm voice, a welcoming tune and a chorus that invites everyone in.
The Beach Boys: The Beach Boys made close harmonies and California pop their calling cards, with songs including “Surfin’ U.S.A.”. Their Christmas recordings bring that sound into colder weather, especially on “Little Saint Nick”. The catalogue here includes its 1991 remix, offering the familiar festive tune in a later mix rather than a different song.
Nat King Cole: Nat King Cole began as a jazz pianist and became a much-loved interpreter of songs, with “Unforgettable” among his signature recordings. His voice is closely associated with “The Christmas Song”, better known to many by its opening mention of chestnuts. It’s an unhurried seasonal welcome, delivered with warmth rather than a need to shout.
Jonas Brothers: Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas built a pop career together before returning from separate projects with the hit “Sucker”. “I Need You Christmas” shows a gentler side of the brothers’ sound. Its nostalgic mood and close vocals offer a quiet seasonal pause, more suited to settling in with the family than starting a kitchen disco.
Jona Lewie: Jona Lewie’s individual approach to pop produced “You’ll Always Find Me in the Kitchen at Parties” and the enduring “Stop the Cavalry”. The latter combines an anti-war message with brass-band colour and a longing to be home at Christmas. It’s an unusual seasonal favourite whose memorable tune carries something more serious beneath the surface.
Barbra Streisand: Barbra Streisand’s career spans the stage, cinema and recording studio, with Funny Girl and “The Way We Were” among its familiar landmarks. Her 1967 release A Christmas Album includes “The Christmas Song” and “The Best Gift”. She brings a storyteller’s attention to these seasonal songs, finding character in the quieter phrases as well as the grand moments.
Bruce Springsteen: Bruce Springsteen built his reputation on vivid songwriting and energetic performances with the E Street Band, with “Born to Run” a defining moment. His rendition of “Santa Claus Is Coming to Town” brings that live-show spirit to Christmas. It sounds like an invitation to join the crowd, rather than a request to sit quietly by the tree.
Robbie Williams: Robbie Williams moved from Take That to a solo career encompassing pop anthems and swing standards. His album The Christmas Present combines seasonal favourites with newer songs, giving that showman’s voice another setting. It’s a natural extension of his taste for entertainment, with room for both a heartfelt delivery and a mischievous change of mood.
Brenda Lee: Brenda Lee’s career embraces rockabilly, pop and country, with hits including “I’m Sorry” and “Sweet Nothin’s”. She recorded “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” in 1958, giving the song a confident swing that still feels inviting. It’s a Christmas party favourite with enough bounce to make standing still beside the buffet quite a challenge.
Dean Martin: Dean Martin balanced singing, films and television with a relaxed performing style that made songs such as “That’s Amore” feel effortless. His seasonal recordings include “Let It Snow! Let It Snow! Let It Snow!”. There’s an easy warmth to his delivery, as though the winter weather is simply an excellent reason to stay indoors.
Andy Williams: Andy Williams became closely associated with “Moon River” and a television career that brought his singing into family homes. His recording of “It’s the Most Wonderful Time of the Year” is another familiar calling card. The bright arrangement and welcoming vocal offer Christmas optimism on a grand scale, without requiring the rest of us to hit every note.
Freya Skye: Freya Skye combines pop singing with screen work, including Disney’s ZOMBIES 4: Dawn of the Vampires. “Snow Angels”, recorded with Malachi Barton, adds a wintry duet to that musical world. Her clear pop delivery gives the song a youthful warmth, offering a different generation’s voice alongside the long-established names on the Christmas playlist.
Cliff Richard: Cliff Richard’s career runs from early rock ’n’ roll with the Shadows to pop favourites including “We Don’t Talk Anymore”. Christmas brought another signature recording in “Mistletoe and Wine”, the UK Christmas number one in 1988. Its traditional imagery and singable chorus offer a familiar seasonal welcome, with room for reflection as well as celebration.
Paul McCartney: Paul McCartney’s songwriting helped define the Beatles, before further success with Wings and his solo recordings. “Wonderful Christmastime”, released in 1979, takes a delightfully uncomplicated approach to the season. Its bouncing synthesiser and easy chorus focus on getting together and enjoying the moment, rather than making Christmas any more complicated than it needs to be.
Mariah Carey: Mariah Carey established her pop and R&B career with songs including “Vision of Love” and “Emotions”. Her 1994 album Merry Christmas introduced “All I Want for Christmas Is You”, pairing a romantic wish with a bustling seasonal arrangement. The opening bells hardly need an introduction now; the high notes may still require a little caution at home.
Elton John: Elton John’s piano-led songwriting and partnership with Bernie Taupin produced songs including “Your Song” and “Rocket Man”. Their 1973 single “Step Into Christmas” brings that exuberance to the festive season. It’s a brisk invitation to celebrate together, with a rolling rhythm that suggests the party has already started before you have found somewhere to put your coat.
Ed Sheeran: Ed Sheeran’s career grew from acoustic songwriting into pop hits including “The A Team”, “Thinking Out Loud” and “Shape of You”. His seasonal recordings include “Under the Tree”, alongside his separate Christmas collaboration with Elton John. Here, the focus is on the more intimate side of his voice, making space for feelings beyond the festivities.
Cher: Cher’s recording career stretches from Sonny & Cher’s “I Got You Babe” to the dance-pop reinvention of “Believe”. “DJ Play a Christmas Song” brings that dance-floor instinct to her album Christmas. It’s a seasonal request with a strong beat behind it, ideal for listeners who would rather celebrate on their feet than sit beside the fire.
Bing Crosby: Bing Crosby brought an intimate singing style to radio, records and films, becoming closely associated with Irving Berlin’s “White Christmas”. His recording offers a wistful picture of the season rather than a noisy celebration. That easy, conversational voice remains the attraction: a little nostalgia for anyone dreaming of snow, wherever they happen to be listening.
Michael Buble: Michael Bublé combines traditional pop and swing with his own songs, following albums such as Crazy Love with Christmas in 2011. His seasonal repertoire includes “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)” and “It’s Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas”. The appeal is in the relaxed phrasing and generous arrangements: familiar songs given room to breathe and swing.
